title: Palpitations: Capture the Rhythm, Stratify the Risk
bottomLine: Palpitations are a symptom, not a rhythm diagnosis. First identify instability and structural-heart red flags, then use the episode pattern, 12-lead ECG and appropriately matched ambulatory monitoring to capture the rhythm before committing to treatment.
recognize: Abrupt regular rapid episodes suggest re-entrant SVT; irregular episodes raise AF/ectopy; pounding with standing, stress, stimulants or hyperthyroidism may be sinus tachycardia or heightened awareness.
Syncope, exertional episodes, family history of sudden death or known cardiomyopathy raises arrhythmic risk.
differentiate: Anxiety can cause palpitations but must not be assumed before cardiac, endocrine, medication and substance causes are considered.
Premature beats may feel dramatic despite low risk, whereas serious arrhythmias can be intermittent and absent on the office ECG.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope/presyncope, exertional relationship, onset/termination, duration, regularity, pregnancy, thyroid symptoms, anemia/bleeding, caffeine/stimulants/decongestants and QT-active medications.
Examine rhythm, murmurs, heart-failure signs and orthostatic physiology when relevant.
workup: Obtain ECG and use targeted CBC/electrolytes/TSH or other tests only when history suggests them.
Match ambulatory monitoring duration to symptom frequency; an event that happens monthly is unlikely to be captured by a very short monitor.
management: Treat the documented rhythm and reversible cause rather than the sensation alone.
Urgent cardiology/ED assessment is warranted for instability, concerning exertional syncope, high-risk ECG findings or ventricular arrhythmia concern.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric rate-slowing therapy in an undiagnosed patient with bradyarrhythmia/conduction disease or pre-excitation concern.
Review stimulant, thyroid, bronchodilator and QT-prolonging exposures before adding antiarrhythmic therapy.
redFlags: Family history of sudden unexplained death
counselling: Teach patients to record pulse/rhythm device data when safe and note triggers/duration rather than repeatedly checking asymptomatic heart rate.
followUp: Close the loop on monitor results and escalate unexplained recurrent symptoms when structural or inherited arrhythmia remains plausible.
examTrap: Diagnosing panic disorder from palpitations before obtaining a basic rhythm and risk assessment.
oneLinePearl: Palpitations become diagnosable when the symptom is linked to the rhythm.
sourceBasis: Canadian Heart Rhythm Society practice resources

title: Cardiomyopathy: Define the Phenotype Before the Treatment Plan
bottomLine: Cardiomyopathy is a structural/functional myocardial phenotype with heterogeneous causes. Define the ventricular phenotype, exclude ischemic/valvular/toxic causes, identify inherited disease when plausible, and treat heart failure/arrhythmic risk while arranging specialty evaluation.
recognize: Dilated, hypertrophic, arrhythmogenic and restrictive/infiltrative patterns have different causes and sudden-death implications.
Family history of cardiomyopathy, sudden death, unexplained syncope or conduction disease raises inherited-disease concern.
differentiate: Ischemic cardiomyopathy must be distinguished from primary nonischemic myocardial disease.
Athlete's heart and hypertension can mimic hypertrophic phenotypes; amyloidosis and other infiltrative disease can mimic hypertrophic/restrictive patterns.
assessment: Assess HF symptoms, arrhythmia/syncope, pregnancy/peripartum timing, alcohol/toxins/chemotherapy, viral/inflammatory illness, neuromuscular/systemic disease and three-generation family history when relevant.
workup: Use ECG, echocardiography and cause-directed labs; CMR helps characterize scar/infiltration and phenotype when indicated.
Ischemic evaluation, genetic counselling/testing and family screening are selected according to phenotype and history.
management: Treat HF according to phenotype and current CCS guidance, manage arrhythmias and refer for device/sudden-death risk assessment when indicated.
Specialty management is required for hypertrophic, arrhythmogenic, infiltrative or rapidly progressive phenotypes and for pregnancy planning in significant disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid medications that worsen obstruction/hypotension in susceptible hypertrophic physiology without specialist context.
Pregnancy and lactation change the safety of RAAS inhibitors and other cardiomyopathy therapies.
counselling: Discuss family screening and activity/pregnancy advice only after phenotype/risk is defined; do not give one universal restriction for every cardiomyopathy.
followUp: Track ventricular function, arrhythmia burden, symptoms and family/genetic actions through cardiology.
examTrap: Calling every reduced EF 'dilated cardiomyopathy' before excluding ischemia, valve disease, toxin and tachycardia causes.
oneLinePearl: Cardiomyopathy management starts with phenotype and cause, not EF alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart failure/cardiomyopathy resources
Canadian inherited heart disease practice principles

title: Aortic Stenosis: Severity Plus Symptoms Determines Urgency
bottomLine: Aortic stenosis becomes high risk when severe valve obstruction produces symptoms, LV dysfunction or other high-risk features. Use echocardiographic severity plus symptoms and functional status; do not rely on murmur intensity or one gradient in isolation.
recognize: Exertional dyspnea, angina, presyncope/syncope and HF are classic symptomatic severe-AS presentations.
Low-flow states can produce discordant valve-area/gradient measurements and require expert echo/hemodynamic interpretation.
differentiate: A soft murmur does not exclude severe AS in low-output states.
Syncope in a patient with AS still requires consideration of arrhythmia, orthostasis and other causes rather than automatic attribution.
assessment: Assess exertional symptoms, syncope, HF, BP, pulse contour, murmur/radiation, frailty, CAD, renal disease and baseline function.
workup: Use transthoracic echocardiography for valve anatomy/severity and LV response; repeat frequency depends on severity and symptoms.
Discordant severe-AS data may require expert echo review, CT calcium assessment, stress testing in selected asymptomatic patients or invasive hemodynamics.
management: Symptomatic severe AS or severe AS with guideline-defined high-risk features warrants structural-heart referral for valve intervention assessment.
Do not delay referral by repeatedly escalating symptom medication in a patient whose fixed obstruction requires definitive treatment.
medicationSafety: Avoid precipitous preload/afterload reduction in unstable severe fixed obstruction; manage hypertension/HF carefully rather than withholding all evidence-based therapy reflexively.
counselling: Explain that the valve problem is mechanical and medications may control associated conditions but do not remove severe obstruction.
followUp: Ensure cardiology/structural-heart follow-up and surveillance interval is documented rather than leaving severe disease on an open-ended repeat-echo plan.
examTrap: Calling severe AS 'stable' because the patient has learned to avoid exertion and therefore denies symptoms.
oneLinePearl: For aortic stenosis, ask what the patient can no longer do—not just whether they volunteer symptoms.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society valvular heart disease resources
CCS Drive/Valvular guidance and structural-heart practice

title: Mitral Valve Prolapse: Separate the Click From Significant Regurgitation
bottomLine: Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign, but risk is driven by the severity of mitral regurgitation, LV/LA response, arrhythmia and symptoms—not by the label or midsystolic click itself. Confirm clinically significant disease with echocardiography and avoid unnecessary antibiotic/activity restrictions.
recognize: MVP can have a midsystolic click and late systolic murmur; significant MR can cause dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, AF or HF.
A flail leaflet or severe MR changes prognosis and referral needs.
differentiate: Palpitations and chest symptoms in MVP are not automatically caused by the valve; arrhythmia and noncardiac causes still require evaluation.
Routine infective-endocarditis prophylaxis is not indicated for uncomplicated MVP.
assessment: Assess exertional symptoms, palpitations/syncope, family history sudden death, murmur characteristics, pregnancy plans and prior echo findings.
workup: Obtain echo when diagnosis/significant MR is suspected; rhythm monitoring is selected for symptomatic palpitations/syncope.
Follow severe MR with guideline-directed imaging/structural-heart evaluation rather than annual testing of every trivial prolapse.
management: Reassure low-risk asymptomatic MVP without significant MR; manage arrhythmia/HF based on the actual syndrome.
Refer severe MR, LV/LA consequences, pulmonary hypertension, AF or concerning symptoms for valve-team evaluation.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe antibiotics before dental procedures solely because MVP is present.
Beta blockers may help selected symptomatic arrhythmias but should not substitute for rhythm diagnosis or severe-MR management.
counselling: Most MVP does not require major lifestyle restriction; counselling should match MR/arrhythmic risk rather than the diagnostic label.
followUp: Surveillance interval follows MR severity and ventricular/atrial response.
examTrap: Giving endocarditis prophylaxis to every patient with MVP before routine dental work.
oneLinePearl: In MVP, the clinically important question is usually 'how much regurgitation and arrhythmic risk?'
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society valvular heart disease resources

title: Advanced ECG Interpretation: Rate, Rhythm, Axis, Intervals, Ischemia, Then Context
bottomLine: A safe ECG interpretation is systematic and clinical: verify rate/rhythm, conduction/intervals, axis, chamber/voltage patterns, ST-T changes and comparison with prior tracing, then decide whether the finding explains the patient's syndrome or requires emergency action.
recognize: ST elevation, high-grade AV block, wide-complex tachycardia, marked QT prolongation and ischemic dynamic change can be time-critical.
Automated ECG interpretation is an aid, not the final diagnosis.
differentiate: Early repolarization/pericarditis/LVH can mimic ischemic ST change; STEMI can be subtle or atypical and must be interpreted with symptoms/serial ECGs.
A wide QRS may reflect bundle-branch block, pacing, pre-excitation, electrolyte/toxic effects or ventricular rhythm.
assessment: Check symptoms, hemodynamics, prior ECG, medications/electrolytes, pacemaker status and lead-placement quality before overinterpreting abnormalities.
workup: Repeat ECG when symptoms evolve; use troponin, electrolytes, echo or rhythm monitoring according to the suspected syndrome.
Do not use one normal ECG to exclude intermittent arrhythmia or early ACS.
management: Treat the clinical syndrome and rhythm stability first; urgent transfer is required for acute ischemic, unstable brady/tachy or malignant electrical patterns.
medicationSafety: Review QT-prolonging and rate-slowing drugs when conduction/QT abnormalities are present.
Electrolyte/toxin causes must be corrected rather than treated as primary arrhythmia alone.
counselling: Avoid telling patients an automated label is a diagnosis before clinician interpretation and clinical correlation.
followUp: Ensure incidental but meaningful conduction/QT/structural clues receive appropriate follow-up rather than being lost after the acute complaint resolves.
examTrap: Choosing the machine-generated ECG diagnosis over a conflicting clinical pattern and tracing review.
oneLinePearl: Read the ECG systematically, then ask whether it explains the patient in front of you.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society rhythm resources

title: Stress Testing: Choose the Test the Patient Can Actually Answer
bottomLine: Stress-test selection depends on the clinical question, pretest likelihood, ability to exercise and baseline ECG interpretability. A positive or negative test changes probability; it does not override a high-risk acute presentation or replace anatomical/functional clarification when results are equivocal.
recognize: Exercise ECG is most useful when the patient can exercise adequately and the resting ECG permits ischemia interpretation.
Stress imaging is preferred when ECG is uninterpretable, exercise capacity is inadequate or additional localization/function information is needed.
differentiate: Stress testing is not the correct first test for active high-risk ACS symptoms.
A low-risk patient with very low pretest probability may gain more harm than benefit from testing because false positives drive downstream procedures.
assessment: Assess symptom stability, ability to exercise, baseline ECG abnormalities, asthma/bronchospasm, arrhythmia, severe valve disease, pregnancy and medication effects.
workup: Choose exercise ECG, stress echo, nuclear testing, CCTA or another modality according to the question and contraindications.
Interpret exercise capacity, symptoms, ECG/imaging response and hemodynamics together rather than focusing on one report label.
management: Escalate high-risk/strongly positive findings and persistent symptoms to cardiology/anatomic evaluation; reassess the diagnosis when test and clinical probability are discordant.
medicationSafety: Pharmacologic stress agents have disease- and agent-specific contraindications; check current protocol rather than memorizing one universal list.
Holding antianginals before testing is protocol/question dependent.
counselling: Explain that a stress test estimates ischemia/risk; it is not a perfect 'yes/no' coronary-disease test.
followUp: Close the loop on abnormal/equivocal results and avoid repeating tests without a new clinical question.
examTrap: Ordering outpatient exercise stress testing for a patient with ongoing suspected ACS who needs emergency evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Pick the stress test that matches the patient, the ECG and the question.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society ischemic heart disease/imaging resources

title: Echocardiography: Translate Measurements Into Hemodynamics
bottomLine: An echocardiogram is a structural/hemodynamic report, not a diagnosis by itself. Integrate EF, chamber size/function, valve severity, pressure estimates and pericardial findings with symptoms, rhythm and loading conditions; refer when the echo reveals a lesion that changes prognosis or intervention timing.
recognize: LVEF does not describe all HF: patients can have HF with EF above 40%, RV failure or important valvular disease.
Valve gradients/regurgitation severity and pulmonary-pressure estimates vary with flow/loading conditions and may require expert review when discordant.
differentiate: A normal EF does not exclude HFpEF, ischemia, constriction or pulmonary vascular disease.
Mild incidental abnormalities should not be treated as the cause of severe symptoms without clinical correlation.
assessment: Review indication, volume/BP/rhythm at the time of study, prior echo, symptoms, murmur, HF/ischemic/arrhythmic context.
workup: Use repeat echo for meaningful clinical change or guideline-directed surveillance, not on a reflex annual schedule for every minor lesion.
Use TEE, CMR/CT or invasive hemodynamics when transthoracic echo cannot answer the clinical question.
management: Treat the underlying HF/valve/pericardial syndrome and refer significant structural disease at the appropriate threshold.
medicationSafety: Do not change chronic HF/valve medications solely from EF without reviewing BP, renal function, congestion and the total syndrome.
counselling: Explain what the echo actually found rather than telling the patient only that the 'EF is normal/low'.
followUp: Document who owns surveillance/referral for significant findings and compare serial studies using the same clinical question.
examTrap: Reassuring a dyspneic patient because EF is normal while ignoring severe diastolic, valve or RV disease.
oneLinePearl: Echo measurements matter only after they are translated into physiology and symptoms.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society imaging/heart failure/valvular resources

title: Cardiac CT and MRI: Use Advanced Imaging to Answer a Specific Question
bottomLine: Cardiac CT and CMR are high-value when they answer a defined anatomic, ischemic, tissue-characterization or structural question. Choose the modality based on the question, renal/contrast/radiation/device considerations and whether the result will change management; do not order advanced imaging as a generic 'better heart test'.
recognize: CCTA can define coronary anatomy and selected structural/aortic questions; CMR excels at ventricular volumes/function, tissue characterization, scar/inflammation and many cardiomyopathies.
Coronary calcium scoring is a risk-refinement tool in selected primary-prevention patients, not an ACS test.
differentiate: CMR and CT are not interchangeable; one may be superior or contraindicated depending on the clinical question.
A normal anatomic test does not explain every chest-pain syndrome, and incidental findings can create downstream testing.
assessment: Define the decision being made, pretest probability, renal function, contrast allergy, pregnancy, rhythm/heart rate, implanted devices/metal and ability to tolerate breath-hold/closed-space imaging.
workup: Use CCTA/CMR after basic evaluation when the result can resolve diagnostic uncertainty or guide treatment; select protocol through imaging/cardiology guidance.
management: Act on clinically meaningful coronary, myocardial, valve/pericardial or aortic findings and avoid treating incidental imaging abnormalities without clinical correlation.
medicationSafety: Iodinated/gadolinium contrast decisions depend on renal function and clinical necessity; follow current contrast guidance rather than blanket avoidance.
Beta-blocker/nitroglycerin use for CCTA is protocol-specific and requires contraindication review.
redFlags: Severe renal/contrast issue when urgent imaging is required
CMR finding suggesting active myocarditis/infiltrative/high-risk cardiomyopathy
counselling: Explain what question the advanced test is designed to answer and why it may not replace other cardiac testing.
followUp: Close the loop on incidental and clinically important findings; do not let an imaging report become an unowned problem list.
examTrap: Ordering cardiac MRI merely because it is 'more detailed' when a simpler test already answers the clinical question.
oneLinePearl: Advanced imaging is only advanced care when it answers the right question.
